Reformations of Judah
ref-or-MAY-shuhnz uhv JOO-duh
noun (historical, redemptive-historical)
From Latin reformare, to form again or restore to a former state; applied to the recurring covenant-renewals of the kings of Judah who turned the nation back to the worship of the LORD.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Reformations of Judah were the recurring seasons of covenant-renewal in which faithful kings of the house of David turned the nation back from idolatry to the worship of the LORD according to His word. Asa took away the altars of strange gods and commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers (2 Chron 14:3-4). Jehoshaphat sent the law of God through the cities and put away the high places. Hezekiah reopened and cleansed the house of the LORD, broke the brasen serpent that had become an idol, and kept a great passover. The pattern reached its height under Josiah, when the book of the law was found in the temple, read before the king, and made the rule of a sweeping purge: "And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments" (2 Kings 23:3). True reform was never innovation but return; it tore down the high places and recovered the buried word. Yet even Josiah's reform could not finally turn away the wrath kindled by Manasseh. This dictionary confesses that all genuine reformation is a return to the word of God, the very principle the Reformers recovered against the corruptions of Rome.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The recurring covenant-renewals under faithful Davidic kings — Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah — who tore down the high places and recovered the book of the law. True reform was always a return to the word, the same principle the Reformation recovered.

expand to see more

REFORMATIONS OF JUDAH, noun. The seasons of covenant-renewal in which godly kings turned the nation back to the worship of the LORD.

They were marked by the casting down of high places, the cleansing of the temple, and the keeping of the passover.

"And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments" (2 Kings 23:3).

True reform requires not innovation but return to the word of God already given.

Their sanction and their limit alike teach that no human reform can finally avert judgment apart from the heart God renews.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Chron 14:4 — "And commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers, and to do the law and the commandment."

2 Kings 18:4 — "He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan."

2 Kings 22:8 — "And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it."

2 Kings 23:3 — "And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The reformations face no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that true reform is always a return to the word of God, never a fresh human invention.

expand to see more

The kings who reformed Judah did not devise new worship; they recovered the old, commanded worship that had been buried under generations of compromise. Josiah's reform began the moment the book of the law was found and read. This is the abiding shape of reformation: the church is purified not by progress beyond Scripture but by return to it, casting down the high places that the inventions of men have raised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that of the Protestant Reformation itself, which was no innovation but a recovery of the gospel and the worship of God from the corruptions of Rome. As Judah's kings tore down the high places and held up the recovered book, so the Reformers held up the open Scripture against will-worship and accumulated tradition. Yet the limit of Josiah's reform — that it could not avert the judgment Manasseh had earned — warns that outward reform must be matched by the heart God alone renews.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word names a re-forming, a return to a former and better state, here the recovery of the LORD's appointed worship.

expand to see more

Reformare — Latin, to form again, to restore what had been marred to its right shape.

In Judah the re-forming meant tearing down high places and altars of strange gods.

It meant the cleansing and reopening of the temple and the keeping of the appointed feasts.

Above all it meant the recovery of the book of the law and submission of king and people to its words.

The same Latin root names the sixteenth-century Reformation, a return to Scripture against the corruptions of Rome.

Usage

"The Reformations of Judah were never novelties but returns to the word the nation had forsaken."

"Hezekiah's reformation broke even the brasen serpent once Moses had made, for it had become an idol."

"Josiah's reformation began the day Shaphan read the recovered book of the law before the king."
